scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

This is a classic case of **emotional labor imbalance**—she’s offloading her own responsibilities onto you while refusing to contribute fairly. 2. **Her Own Neglect**: She’s been passive in cooking for years (even when your dad tried to teach her), and now she’s suddenly expecting *you* to step up without any reciprocity. This is hypocritical. If she wants dinner, she should cook it—especially since she’s the one who’s been avoiding it for so long. 3. **Your Dad’s Role**: The fact that your dad is doing *all* the cooking (even late at night) while your mom does nothing is a red flag. This isn’t just about dinner—it’s about **who in the household is expected to do the emotional and physical labor**. You’re not wrong for calling this out, even if it’s uncomfortable. 4. **Your Own Efforts**: You’ve already been cooking and baking for weeks, which is commendable. But if she’s now demanding *daily* meals without acknowledging the effort you’ve already put in, that’s unreasonable. 5. **Her Reaction Was Unjustified**: She screamed at you for not cooking, but she never asked *why* you weren’t cooking. She also never considered that you have schoolwork. Her anger was disproportionate and unfair—especially since she’s the one who’s been avoiding cooking for years. --- ### **Why This Situation Is "Wrong" (Systemically):** 1. **Gendered Expectations**: Women (and daughters) are often expected to handle cooking and domestic labor without recognition or fairness. This is unfair and sets a bad precedent. 3. **Emotional Manipulation**: Her reaction ("she’s ashamed of us") is guilt-tripping, which is a common tactic to silence dissent. You’re not "useless"—she’s the one who’s been neglectful. 4. **Your Dad’s Sacrifice**: The fact that your dad is doing all the cooking (even late at night) while your mom does nothing is a **huge** imbalance. This isn’t just about dinner—it’s about **who in the household is expected to do the emotional and physical labor**. If she wants dinner, she should cook it—especially since she’s the one who’s been avoiding it for years. --- ### **What You Could Do Moving Forward:** 1. **Set Boundaries (Politely but Firmly)**: - You don’t *have* to cook every night, especially if you have schoolwork. If she wants dinner, she can cook it (or at least help). - Example: *"Mom, I’ve been doing a lot of cooking lately, but I also have a lot of schoolwork. If you want dinner, I can help, but I can’t cook every night. Maybe you can take turns?"* 2. **Call Out the Inequity**: - *"You’ve never cooked before, but now you expect me to? Dad does all the cooking, and you never help. It’s not fair."* - This might make her defensive, but it’s important for her to see the imbalance. 3. **Involve Your Dad**: - Since he’s the one doing most of the cooking, he should be part of the conversation. Maybe he can step in more often, or at least help with the emotional labor of managing meals. 4. **Protect Your Mental Health**: - If she keeps yelling at you, it’s okay to say, *"I’m not comfortable with this tone. Let’s talk about it calmly."* You deserve respect. 5. **Find a Compromise**: - Maybe she can cook on certain days, or you can take turns. Or she can at least help with simple meals (like microwaving something or assembling a salad). --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Not "Wrong," but the Situation Is)** You’re **not wrong** for refusing to cook today—especially given the context. However, the **system** (her expectations, the imbalance in the household, and the lack of accountability) is what’s wrong. You’re being asked to fill a role that’s been neglected for years, and that’s unfair. **You deserve:** ✅ Fairness (she should cook too). ✅ Respect (no yelling or guilt-tripping). ✅ Recognition for your efforts (you’ve already been cooking a lot). If she keeps pushing this, you might need to have a bigger conversation with your dad about how this dynamic is affecting you. You’re not just a "daughter"—you’re a student with responsibilities, and she shouldn’t expect you to drop everything for her. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to her (or your dad) about this? You’re handling this situation with a lot of maturity—it’s clear you care about fairness.
